paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a configurable from-scratch generator and benchmark for evaluating numerical question answering over multiple non-relational (pivoted/perturbed) tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + instances) via LLM prompting, derives executable SQL queries on that source to compute verifiable gold answers, then renders multiple perturbed non-relational views (hierarchical pivots, merged headers, blank rows, typographical noise, unit conversions, OCR artifacts, etc.) while preserving provenance for answer verification. It supports two multi-table evidence-flow patterns: parallel (extract one scalar per view then aggregate) and sequential (lookup chains across tables). The pipeline also includes LLM-based NL question verbalization with a verification pass, and optional SMT-backed semantic constraints during source instantiation. Experiments in financial and environmental domains evaluate several LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen family), demonstrating sharp performance drops as table count and unit heterogeneity increase; sequential chains are harder than parallel aggregation. The paper also shows GRADINO-generated data can augment scarce in-domain supervision.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel, well-motivated generator that fills an important gap: controlled, verifiable multi-table QA over non-relational table renderings. 2) Methodologically principled: decoupling latent SQL supervision from presentation preserves verifiable answers while enabling realistic perturbations. 3) Thorough empirical analysis across models, table counts, domains, unit settings, and reasoning topologies, convincingly exhibiting a critical blind spot for current LLMs. 4) Demonstrates practical utility beyond evaluation: synthetic GRADINO data complements scarce in-domain training data. 5) Good engineering artifacts and reproducibility effort: prompts, constraint machinery, and manual reliability checks are provided.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism: GRADINO trades real-world fidelity for controlled diagnostics. Some real non-relational cues (rich visual alignment, chart-table mixtures, varied OCR artifacts, more complex merged-cell patterns) are not fully modeled, so benchmark instances may not capture the full distribution of real documents. 2) Generator dependence on an LLM: schema, constraints, and questions are LLM-produced, which may introduce stylistic/bias artifacts and raises reproducibility concerns for groups without the same model access. 3) Limited evaluation breadth: more diverse closed and open LLMs and a small human baseline would help contextualize difficulty. 4) Sequential-instance simplification: enforcing unique lookup-key occurrences (one occurrence per intermediate view) reduces ambiguity and may underrepresent realistic multi-join complexities. 5) Candidate filtering bias: a nontrivial fraction of generated candidates is discarded; the impact of this filtering on difficulty distribution deserves more analysis. 6) Narrow question class: focus on scalar aggregations (sum/avg/max/min) excludes richer analytical queries (conditional/group-by/textual aggregation). 7) Finetuning experiments are limited in scale (capped small sets) and models; more scale-ups would strengthen claims about utility for training.
comments_suggestions_typos: Suggestions: (a) Provide a brief pilot human-evaluation (small sample) to indicate how readable/answerable the hardest perturbed instances are for people. (b) Add or emphasize statistics on discarded candidates and show whether discarded instances are systematically harder or of a particular type. (c) Consider an optional harder sequential variant permitting ambiguous lookup-key occurrences (with multiple matches) to test join-disambiguation. (d) Report per-model run variance (error bars) for the zero-shot inference numbers, not only for finetuning. (e) Clarify compute/cost requirements for dataset generation and finetuning to help reproducibility. Minor: ensure consistent capitalization of model names in text; otherwise the manuscript is clear and well organized.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss limitations (synthetic realism, numerical scope limited to scalar aggregations, question generation errors) and ethical considerations (no PII; synthetic content; use of public tables only for validation). They also note interpretive risk: synthetic benchmarks should not be taken as guarantees of real-world robustness. I would encourage expanding discussion on distributional gaps (e.g., cross-lingual tables, domain lexicon coverage) and the potential for generator-induced biases in downstream finetuning.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical issues identified. The paper uses synthetic, fictional data for generated benchmarks, relies on public datasets only for validation, and discusses privacy/ethics. The authors acknowledge limitations and potential misinterpretation risks. I see no ACL Code of Ethics violations.
